What does a Chattanooga seller need to understand first?

Chattanooga is the Hamilton County seat on the Tennessee River, and its housing market is split between owners and a large renter base. QuickFacts shows owners in 52.4 percent of homes for 2020 to 2024, with a typical owned home valued at $283,200. The July 1, 2025 estimate of 194,144 residents sits 6.9 percent above the April 2020 estimates base.

The city covers about 142 square miles of land, so conditions change a lot between neighborhoods. Missionary Ridge cuts the city in two several miles east of downtown, Walden's Ridge rises across the river, and the downtown sits at roughly 676 feet. A house on a ridge, in a river-side flood area or in a historic district faces different buyer questions, and your sale plan should start with where the lot sits.

Sellers who want speed usually weigh an as-is cash purchase against a conventional listing. The cash route drops repairs, showings and appraisal conditions. A listing may bring a higher price for a tidy house when the calendar allows.

Which Chattanooga neighborhoods and districts shape resale?

Historic designation can shape what a buyer may do with a house. Three neighborhoods, Ferger Place, Fort Wood and St. Elmo, carry federal historic-register listings, and the city also has local historic districts including Battery Place, Glenwood, Missionary Ridge, M.L. King and Stringer's Ridge. Ask the Land Development Office whether a local district covers your address before you promise a buyer any exterior renovation.

  • Downtown and the North Shore sit near the Tennessee Aquarium, the Walnut Street Bridge and Coolidge Park.
  • St. Elmo and Fort Wood are two of those register neighborhoods, and the M.L. King district runs beside the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga campus.
  • Hixson, Highland Park and Lookout Valley, also called Tiftonia, are separate communities within the city limits.
  • East of Missionary Ridge, Brainerd Road and East Brainerd Road carry traffic toward Hamilton Place.

Public schools fall under Hamilton County Schools, formed in the 1997 merger of the city and county systems. Ask your listing agent or buyer which zone a given address falls in before quoting school information.

Does Chattanooga's weather and terrain affect a house sale?

Yes, mainly through flooding history, tornado risk and heat. The river's worst flood came in 1867, and the Tennessee Valley Authority reservoir system created after 1933 now regulates it; the highest stage since then, about 37 feet, came in 1973. The climate adds 52 days a year of 90-degree weather or hotter and more than 52 inches of annual precipitation.

Tornadoes have hit the area too. An EF3 tornado struck southeastern Chattanooga on the night of April 12, 2020. Inspectors working for buyers check roof condition, tree cover and drainage, and a seller who has fixed those items in advance gets a cleaner negotiation.

Hilly lots bring their own checks, and a seller can prepare a short file for them:

  • Retaining wall and drainage work, with contractor invoices.
  • Engineer letters on foundations built on sloped ground.
  • Driveway grade and access details for steep lots.

Keep that file ready so it can go out with the first offer.

How much is Chattanooga property tax and when is it due?

The City Council sets the city rate, listed at $1.93 per hundred dollars of assessed value on the city's tax information page. The assessment ratio is 25 percent for homes and 40 percent for commercial parcels, so a $283,200 house, the Census value for an owned home here, carries $70,800 of assessed value and a city bill near $1,366. Hamilton County taxes come on top.

Notices go out in September, taxes are due October 1, and payment stays penalty-free until February's final day. From March 1, interest and penalty total 1.5 percent a month. Prior-year delinquent taxes are filed in Hamilton County Chancery Court each March, and the city says a property can be sold after three years of delinquency.

Chattanooga tax arithmetic on a $283,200 house, the Census median value. Sources: City of Chattanooga, Tennessee Department of Revenue
StepFigure

Assessed value$70,800
City rate$1.93 per $100
City tax per yearabout $1,366

The City Treasurer can be reached at 423-643-7262 and is located at Room 100, 101 E. 11th Street. No state rule obliges the city to mail a notice, which means a lost bill is no defense for paying late. Pull a copy from the city's property tax search before closing.

What can seniors do to freeze Chattanooga city taxes?

Homeowners 65 or older can apply for the city's Tax Freeze, which holds the city portion of the bill steady for one year. The application page sets a combined 2025 income limit of $63,470 and says the home must be the primary residence. The 2026 application deadline is April 5, 2027.

The freeze covers city taxes only. County taxes and fees such as stormwater are not frozen, and the owner has to reapply every year or the taxes revert to the current rate and value. Applicants submit proof of ownership, residency, age and income, and the Senior Programs line is 423-643-7274.

Until closing day, keep the application current, since a lapse returns your city bill to the current rate and value.

How do I dispute a Hamilton County value?

Request an informal review from the Hamilton County Assessor of Property first. The county's reappraisal page lists useful proof: sales prices of similar properties in the immediate area within the last three years, a recent private appraisal and photos. The 2026 informal review window is closed, and results are mailed.

Phone the Assessor at 423-209-7300, weekdays between 8 and 4:30, to ask about the next cycle. The city's tax page says properties are reappraised every four years and that the equalization board at the county takes appeals when the informal review fails, reached at the same number.

After a denial at the county level, the state's appeal guide allows a filing until August 1 of the tax year or within 45 days of the local notice, whichever is later.

Does Chattanooga let me host short-term guests before I sell?

Only with a city certificate, and the zoning rules are tight. The Short-Term Vacation Rental page says every host needs a certificate. A homestay is owner-occupied for at least 183 days a year and costs $250 to apply or renew. An absentee rental costs $500 and is allowed only in commercial zones C-C, C-R, C-MU1 and C-MU2 and form-based zones CC, CX, IX, RF, RV and SH.

Certificates last one year and the Board of Zoning Appeals cannot exceed the 25 percent density cap. Applications have a 60-day life from submission, and a rezoned property cannot get an absentee certificate for 18 months. For a seller, the useful rule is that a valid certificate can be transferred to a new owner of the same address, though the occupancy type cannot change. Call the Land Development Office at 423-643-5891 with questions.

Where do Chattanooga deeds get filed and what does the state charge?

Register Marc Gravitt's office, in the courthouse at 625 Georgia Avenue (Room 400), takes Chattanooga deeds at 423-209-6560 on weekdays from 8 until 4. Its stated duty is to record deeds and similar instruments and to collect the fees and taxes attached to them.

The state's realty transfer tax is 37 cents per $100 of price, which makes about $1,048 on a $283,200 sale. A separate mortgage tax of 11.5 cents per $100 applies to borrowed amounts above the first $2,000. Request the full cost list from the title company before the closing date.

More questions about Chattanooga, TN

How soon can a Chattanooga cash sale close?

Closing is possible within about two weeks when title is clear and any estate or lien paperwork is ready. The Hamilton County Register of Deeds files the deed after signing. Delays usually come from payoff letters and co-owner signatures.

What is the Chattanooga city property tax rate?

The city's tax page lists $1.93 per hundred dollars of assessed value, with homes assessed at 25 percent of appraisal. Hamilton County tax is separate, so ask the Trustee at 423-209-7270 for the county rate.

Who covers the state transfer tax on a Chattanooga sale?

The rate is 37 cents per $100 of price, collected at recording. Your purchase contract says who is responsible, and the title company shows the amount on the closing statement.

Does a vacation rental certificate pass to a buyer?

Yes. It can move to the new owner of the same property when the buyer files the transfer application. It cannot follow the operator to a different address, and the occupancy type stays the same.

When does Hamilton County reappraise next?

The city's tax page says properties are reappraised every four years. Call the Hamilton County Assessor at 423-209-7300 for the next effective date.

What makes selling a house in Clarksville, TN different?

Clarksville is the Montgomery County seat and sits about ten miles from Fort Campbell, where the 101st Airborne Division is stationed. QuickFacts lists 22,758 veterans for 2020 to 2024 and estimates 188,829 residents on July 1, 2025, a 13.2 percent rise over the April 2020 estimates base.

Owners live in 55.6 percent of homes, a typical owned home is valued at $263,600, and typical rent is $1,307. Only 9.6 percent of residents are 65 or older, against 17.3 percent in Chattanooga. A seller with permanent change of station orders may have a firm report date, and speed then outweighs squeezing out the last few thousand dollars.

A cash purchase on an as-is basis removes repair negotiation, showings and buyer financing from that clock. A conventional listing works when the house is move-in ready and the move date is flexible.

What does Clarksville look like on the map?

The city grew up where the Red River meets the Cumberland River, on the northwest edge of the Highland Rim about 45 miles from Nashville. It was founded in 1785, incorporated in 1807 and named for General George Rogers Clark. Austin Peay State University and the oldest newspaper in Tennessee, The Leaf-Chronicle, are based here.

The city spans 99.4 square miles of land with 1,677 residents per square mile, the highest density among Tennessee's four cities profiled here. Main routes include U.S. 41A, which runs as Madison Street and Fort Campbell Boulevard, U.S. 79 along Wilma Rudolph Boulevard, Interstate 24 and State Route 76. The average commute is 27.0 minutes, the longest of the four.

The Clarksville-Montgomery County School System runs the public schools, 39 of them, eight being high schools. Portions of the city on Fort Campbell use the Department of Defense Education Activity. Industrial employers listed for the city include Trane, Amazon, Google, LG, Hankook and Bridgestone.

Do Clarksville storms and floods change how a house sells?

They can, since the city has a recent record of damaging weather and buyers remember it. A tornado ranked F3 hit downtown in January 1999, an EF2 struck the east side in February 2018, and the May 2010 floods damaged the city. In December 2023 an EF3 tornado crossed North Clarksville, killed four people and left more than 20,000 customers without power.

What this means in practice for a seller:

  • Keep roof, siding and window receipts, and note any insurance claim paid for storm damage.
  • Keep permits for repairs made after a storm, since a buyer's inspector will compare work to paperwork.
  • If the house was damaged and not fully repaired, describe the condition to buyers in writing and consider an as-is sale.
  • Check the flood risk for low lots near the Red River and Cumberland River before setting a price.

Cash buyers price the repairs they find, so an honest description up front speeds an offer.

How are Clarksville property taxes billed and paid?

Clarksville and Montgomery County send separate bills. The city builds its bills from the county assessor's file, which lists the person who held title on January 1. Notices mail in October, payment is accepted from October 1 until the final day of February, and after that interest runs at 1.5 percent a month, or 18 percent a year, according to the city's property tax FAQ.

The city tells owners to read their closing documents to see who owes the taxes, because a property can still go to a tax auction if the taxes stay unpaid, whoever was supposed to pay. After a year of delinquency the city turns the account over to a delinquent tax attorney, and payments are then made at the Clerk and Master's office in Montgomery Chancery Court at 2 Millennium Plaza, Number 101.

Payment options at the city level are:

  • In person at Finance and Revenue, One Public Square, Suite 119.
  • At the North Center, 111 Cunningham Lane.
  • By mail to P.O. Box 30549, Clarksville, TN 37040, with the bill stub.
  • Online, which carries a 2.5 percent processing fee.

If a lender and an owner both pay, the city refunds the party that paid second. Call 931-645-7436 with questions. Ask Finance and Revenue at 931-645-7437 for the current city rate.

What tax relief can a Clarksville homeowner use?

The city lists two kinds of relief: one for elderly or disabled homeowners and one for disabled veterans and their surviving spouses. A first-time applicant signs up at the Montgomery County Trustee or at the City of Clarksville Finance and Revenue office, not both. The Trustee is at Veterans Plaza, 350 Pageant Lane, Suite 101-B, phone 931-648-5717.

Those approved for the age or disability category receive a voucher each year with the county and city bills and must bring income records to the city. Veteran-category recipients send signed vouchers to both the city and the county. The state remits its share only when those vouchers come in.

The same Trustee office handles the Tax Freeze program, and the county notifies the city of an approved freeze. Ask the Trustee which documents each program requires before you apply.

Which Clarksville home rules can delay a sale?

City codes matter when an inspection turns up violations. The Codes Enforcement Division reviews property maintenance rules, takes complaints and offers a housing inspection request form. Its public FAQ says vehicles may not park on grass and must sit on concrete, asphalt or gravel. A fence taller than six feet needs a permit, and fences on a residential lot follow 30 or 40 foot front setbacks.

Pools get particular attention. Outdoor residential pools need a barrier at least 48 inches high, gates that close and latch themselves, and openings that stop a 4-inch sphere. Check an older pool and any fence near the setback line against these rules before a buyer's inspector does.

To confirm a lot's zoning, call Building and Codes at 931-645-7426, and call the Regional Planning Commission at 931-645-7448 about rezoning. Close any open complaint before listing.

Where does a Clarksville deed get recorded and what does it cost?

Deeds go to the Montgomery County Register of Deeds, 350 Pageant Lane, Suite 101-A, phone 931-648-5713, where the counter opens at 7:30 in the morning and closes at 4:30 on weekdays. Its FAQ says the office cannot prepare documents or run title searches, requires original signed and notarized documents, asks for the preparer's name and address, and requires an oath of consideration on transfers unless a statute exempts the instrument.

Clarksville recording points. Sources: Montgomery County Register of Deeds, Tennessee Department of Revenue

Both state rates come from the Department of Revenue. The title company totals the recording costs and delivers the signed deed to the office.

More questions about Clarksville, TN

Can I sell my Clarksville house quickly if I have PCS orders?

Yes. With clear title, a cash purchase can be set for a date you pick, frequently about two weeks out. Gather a payoff statement, the deed and any co-owner details. A written closing date lets you plan the move around your report date.

Who pays Clarksville property tax at closing?

On the closing statement the title company splits the year's tax between buyer and seller according to the contract. The city bill goes to the January 1 owner. Read your closing documents so you know who sends payment, because unpaid taxes can end in a tax auction.

Which office records a deed for a Clarksville house?

The Montgomery County Register of Deeds, 350 Pageant Lane, Suite 101-A, phone 931-648-5713. Originals with signatures and notary acknowledgments are required, plus the oath of consideration on most transfers.

What does the state charge on a Clarksville home sale?

The realty transfer tax is 37 cents per $100 of price, about $975 on a $263,600 sale. An 11.5 cent mortgage tax per $100 applies to secured debt above the first $2,000. Both appear on the closing statement.

Is there property tax relief for Clarksville seniors?

Yes. The city and county offer relief for elderly and disabled homeowners and for disabled veterans, plus the Tax Freeze program. Apply at the Montgomery County Trustee, 931-648-5717, or at City Finance and Revenue, 931-645-7436, but not at both.

Where is Franklin, Tennessee, and how fast has it grown?

Williamson County's government sits in Franklin, about 21 miles south of Nashville along the Harpeth River, and only six Tennessee cities have more people. The Census Bureau lists 62,487 people in 2010, 83,454 in 2020 and 90,226 in its July 2025 estimate, an increase of 8.0 percent over the 2020 base. The city covers 42.75 square miles of land, which works out to roughly 1,952 residents per square mile at the 2020 count.

Franklin's population is more than five times what it was in 1980, when 12,407 people lived here. That rise came as northern Franklin filled with houses and offices, and as the city became a Nashville suburb with its own jobs. Anyone thinking about selling a Franklin house is working in a city that has changed fast within a single generation.

What in Franklin's history still shows up in its houses?

Abram Maury Jr. founded the town on October 26, 1799, and named it for Benjamin Franklin. The Second Battle of Franklin on November 30, 1864 produced nearly 10,000 casualties and turned forty-four buildings into temporary field hospitals. The Carter, Carnton and Lotz houses from that era still stand.

Five of the city's historic districts carry National Register listings, and older buildings and neighborhoods get protection under local ordinance. A former stove factory, the Dortch Stove Works of 1928 that later made Magic Chef ranges, was restored in the late 1990s and now holds offices, restaurants and retail space.

An owner near the square or inside a historic district should ask City Hall which rules apply before planning exterior repairs.

Which employers and roads support Franklin's housing market?

Franklin has a deep base of health care and corporate employers. The city's 2024 annual financial report ranks its ten biggest employers, and the top five are below.

Interstate 65 crosses the eastern side of the city with four exits, and US 31 and US 431 run together toward Nashville. State Routes 96, 246 and 441 fan out from Franklin, and the Mack Hatcher Parkway bypass circles the business district to the east. Cool Springs Boulevard and McEwen Drive both have interchanges with I-65.

The city's 2026-27 budget message says a 10-year capital plan of $458 million is 82 percent devoted to transportation, including a state partnership to widen Mack Hatcher Parkway Southeast, the widening of McEwen Road and a new City Hall on the downtown square.

What do Census numbers say about Franklin homes?

QuickFacts puts the typical Franklin owner-occupied house at $705,400 for the 2020 to 2024 period, more than double the $332,700 national median. Owners with a mortgage report monthly costs of $2,542, and owners without one report $712. Renters pay a median of $1,923. Of the city's 33,998 households, 63.8 percent own their home.

Household income has a median of $119,528, and 64.5 percent of residents past age 25 have finished at least a bachelor's degree. About 84.6 percent of people were at the same address a year before the survey. Those figures describe a market with long-staying owners and large price tags.

What does a Franklin homeowner pay in property tax?

The city charges $0.296 for each $100 of assessed value, and the proposed 2026-27 budget leaves that unchanged. The rate has two parts: a $0.2310 base for operations and debt, plus $0.0650 added after the last reappraisal for infrastructure and city services. The city calls its rate one of the lowest in Tennessee. The county assessor reappraises every four years.

The Williamson County Trustee bills for the county, the Franklin Special School District and the city together. Here is how the county's published schedule works:

  • Statements are mailed in early October.
  • Payment opens the first Monday of October and stays open through the end of February.
  • From March 1, a 1.5 percent interest charge starts, then repeats on the first of every later month.
  • The trustee cannot waive, prorate or release any tax or interest.
  • Whoever owned the property on January 1 is the owner of record who gets the bill, so a seller closing mid-year must pass it on to the buyer.

As an example, a Franklin house assessed at 25 percent of a $700,000 value carries $175,000 of assessed value, and the city's share comes to $518. County and school charges are on top of that, so ask the trustee at 615-790-5709 for the full figure on a specific parcel.

Which schools and colleges serve Franklin?

Most of the city belongs to the Franklin Special School District for kindergarten through eighth grade, and high school students attend Williamson County Schools. Outlying parts of the city are in the county district for every grade.

  • Private schools include Battle Ground Academy, Franklin Classical School, Franklin Christian Academy, Montessori School of Franklin, New Hope Academy and Thales Academy.
  • Higher education includes the Columbia State Community College campus that opened in 2016, a Belmont University campus at the Williamson Center, a Lipscomb University SPARK site, New College Franklin and Williamson College.

Families often start a house search with the school boundary, so a seller should be ready to tell a buyer which district serves the address.

What city fees and utilities will a Franklin buyer ask about?

Buyers often ask about monthly costs, and Franklin's budget documents answer part of the question. The buyer does, as the grantee on the deed. The state rate is 37 cents per $100 of price, collected by the register at filing.

Where is Gallatin, Tennessee, and how did it start?

The Cumberland River runs past Gallatin, which serves as Sumner County's seat and lies roughly 30 miles northeast of Nashville. Settlers secured the land along Station Camp Creek early, and Captain William Asher built a fortified station there in 1780. The town was established in 1802 and named for Albert Gallatin, the Treasury Secretary under Jefferson and Madison. Andrew Jackson bought one of the first lots after the 1803 survey, and the town incorporated in 1815.

The Union Army took the town in February 1862 because of its railroad and river position, and Union troops occupied it for the rest of the war. A cholera epidemic hit in the summer of 1873. The calendar includes the Sumner County Fair in the last week of August, a Fall Festival on the square, a Christmas parade and a Candlelight Cemetery Tour on the first Saturday of October. The Palace, a single-screen theater from 1908, has been restored. Historic buildings that survive include Cragfont, Rosemont and Trousdale Place, and the city has a central historic district.

How fast is Gallatin growing?

Gallatin has grown quickly. The Census Bureau counted 30,278 people in 2010 and 44,431 in 2020, and its July 2025 estimate is 54,590, a 22.8 percent jump from the 2020 base. Land area is 32.17 square miles.

That pace of growth is the background to the new zoning ordinance the city adopted in 2026, covered below, and to the Station Camp and Liberty Creek school campuses on the list further down.

Which employers keep Gallatin's housing market moving?

Gallatin's largest named employers and projects include:

  • Gap, Inc., with 1,250 workers, plus Sumner Regional Medical Center (now Highpoint Health), Volunteer State Community College and RR Donnelley
  • Beretta, the Italian gunmaker, which moved its US production here in 2015
  • Meta, whose data center of more than 1.6 million square feet opened in 2020, with a 2024 expansion announced to lift its Gallatin investment past $1 billion
  • The Tennessee Valley Authority, which operates a coal-fired power plant in the city

Highpoint Health, the former Sumner Regional Medical Center, operates an emergency room, a cancer program, a wound care center and a cardiac catheterization lab. Vol State, part of the Tennessee Board of Regents system, has its main campus in Gallatin and has drawn more than 150,000 students since 1971. Sumner County's unemployment rate was 2.8 percent in March 2025.

What do Census figures say about houses in Gallatin?

QuickFacts lists a $372,000 median value for Gallatin's owned homes in the 2020 to 2024 survey, above the national $332,700 and well below Franklin's $705,400. Monthly costs for owners are $1,778 with a loan and $552 without. Rent has a median of $1,395. Among 19,755 households, 57.1 percent own.

The household income median is $77,518, the poverty rate is 13.0 percent, and 33.5 percent of people past 25 hold a bachelor's degree.

Which roads and schools matter to Gallatin buyers?

US 31E, also called Nashville Pike or Gallatin Road, is the main street through town. State Route 386, Vietnam Veterans Boulevard, is a controlled-access road that ends in Gallatin and links to Interstate 65. State Routes 109 and 25 complete the network, and WeGo Public Transit runs a daily bus to downtown Nashville. Sumner County Regional Airport has a 5,000-foot runway.

The Sumner County Board of Education runs Gallatin's public schools, and these campuses serve the city:

  • High schools: Gallatin High, Station Camp High and Liberty Creek High
  • Middle schools: Joe Shafer, Liberty Creek, Station Camp and Rucker-Stewart
  • Elementary schools: Benny Bills, Guild, Howard, Liberty Creek, Station Camp, Union STEM and Vena Stuart

The county system had about 29,400 students in 49 schools as of August 2020. Old Hickory Lake and six city parks add recreation, including Lock 4, Triple Creek and Thompson parks.

How are Gallatin property taxes set and paid?

For 2026 the city charges $0.5295 on each $100 of assessed value, using values from the Sumner County assessor. Payment is due before March 1, when interest begins. Tennessee law does not require mailed notices, so an unreceived bill is no defense. Payment plans can be arranged through the Recorder's Office.

The city offers relief for qualifying elderly homeowners, disabled homeowners and disabled veteran or widow homeowners, and a tax freeze program that must be recertified every year through the Sumner County Trustee.

Sumner County reappraises every five years. The last reappraisal was 2024 and the next is scheduled for 2029. An owner who disputes a value begins with an informal review at the assessor's office. The next step is the county Board of Equalization, in session from June 1. Beyond that sits the State Board, with a deadline of August 1 or 45 days after the local notice, whichever falls later.

Gallatin adopted a new zoning ordinance and zoning map effective September 1, 2026, so older notes on a lot's zoning may be out of date. The Planning Department also handles fences, signs, temporary use permits and flood zone questions. Its commission and zoning appeals board work on a six-week review cycle.

Building permits are applied for through the city's Citizens Self-Service Portal. Contractors must email permits@gallatintn.gov a copy of their state license, general liability and workers' compensation insurance or a state exemption, and a signed city permit bond with a power of attorney before they can apply.

If a past owner finished a basement or added a room, ask the city permit office at permits@gallatintn.gov whether permits were closed. A buyer's lender and inspector will ask the same question.

How is a Gallatin deed recorded?

Deeds for Gallatin houses go to the Sumner County Register of Deeds on North Belvedere Drive. Weekday hours are 8 to 4:30, and a typical year brings in more than 30,000 recorded documents. It accepts electronic filing through Simplifile and CSC, and it offers a free MyLandAlert notice that emails an owner when a document is recorded under their name.

The register collects the state conveyance tax, set by Revenue at 37 cents per $100 of price and owed by the grantee. Records are certified back to September 1989 and can be searched online, and deed books and indexes have been digitized back to 1786.

An heir or a seller in a hurry should have a title company confirm the chain of recorded deeds before a closing date is set.

Selling to a direct cash buyer is fastest, because the buyer arranges no loan and takes the property without any fixes. An agent listing is still worth pricing out in Collierville, since a house in top shape can draw strong bids, but it brings preparation, showings and a lender's calendar.

Collierville holds the legal status of a town and sits in Shelby County within the Memphis metropolitan area. The Census Bureau counted 51,324 residents in 2020 and puts the July 1, 2025 estimate at 51,909. Wikipedia lists it third among Shelby County municipalities, after Memphis and Bartlett.

The Census paints Collierville as a family town. Children under 18 are 26.8% of residents, homes hold 2.82 people on average, and 89.1% of people stayed at one address across a year. Residents who are Asian alone account for 13.8%, and 13.5% were born abroad.

What is the story behind the Collierville town square?

Jesse R. Collier laid out the settlement in 1836, which makes Collierville the second oldest town in Shelby County. It was chartered in 1850. Union and Confederate forces fought twice here in 1863, on October 11 and again on November 3, and the original settlement was destroyed. The town was rechartered in 1870.

The historic downtown is a National Register listing, and Parade magazine named the square the Best Main Street in America in 2014. The Carriage Crossing shopping mall also sits in town. Wikipedia gives the town 24.5 square miles of land, while the Census Bureau lists 36.32 square miles for 2020, a sign that boundaries have expanded.

  • Interstate 269 and State Route 385 (Nonconnah and Bill Morris Parkway) connect to Memphis.
  • Poplar Avenue carries U.S. 72 and State Route 57.
  • State Route 175 appears as Byhalia Road, Collierville Road and South Houston Levee Road.
  • State Route 205 is the Collierville-Arlington Road.

How do spring storms affect a Collierville house sale?

The climate here is humid subtropical, hot and sticky from late May to late September. Wikipedia calls spring the severe weather season, with April historically the peak month for tornadoes, although tornadoes have been recorded in every month.

Rain and melted snow add up to roughly 57 inches in a normal year (1991 to 2020), and July highs average 91.4 degrees. Because storms are part of local life, buyers ask about roof age, hail damage and drainage near the foundation.

If you replaced a roof or fixed wind damage, keep the invoice and any insurance claim file. A lender or insurer may request it, and a cash buyer will use it to set the price.

How do the town and county tax bills work in Collierville?

A Collierville owner is billed by the Town of Collierville and by Shelby County. Under the town's worked example, a $100,000 home is assessed at 25%, or $25,000, and the $1.62 rate per $100 produces a $405 town bill. The town's tax department answers at 901-457-2281.

The Shelby County Trustee sets payment from the first Monday of October to the last day of February. Collierville is listed, along with Shelby County, with a March 1 delinquency date, and unpaid balances pick up 1.5% interest monthly, or 18% yearly. Mail must carry a postmark by the last day of February, and Trustee Customer Service is at 901-222-0200.

If no will was probated, the register says an affidavit of heirship is the document to file.

  • Locate the death certificate, the will if there is one, and the last deed.

Where is Germantown, Tennessee?

Germantown is an eastern suburb of Memphis in Shelby County, covering just under 20 square miles of land. The city grew on a ridge between the Wolf River and Nonconnah Creek, about 16 miles east of the Mississippi River. It has its own mayor-alderman government, with a mayor and five part-time aldermen elected to four-year terms, and a professional city administrator who handles daily operations.

Annual events include the Germantown Charity Horse Show in June and the Germantown Festival, an arts and crafts fair, in early September. The Arbor Day Foundation has named it a Tree City USA for 33 consecutive years.

In 2019 the city won the Malcolm Baldrige National Quality Award, and Wikipedia notes only five municipalities have ever received it. A seller's day-to-day contact with the city is more practical: tax statements, code compliance and a design review process for exterior changes.

How did Germantown get its name and its look?

Settlers arrived around 1825. The area was called Pea Ridge from 1833, town lots were laid out in 1834, and the name changed to Germantown in 1836 to reflect German families nearby. The town was chartered in 1841, and the Memphis and Charleston Railroad came through in 1852. Yellow fever epidemics between 1867 and 1878 cut the population roughly in half.

The name briefly changed to Neshoba, a Chickasaw word for wolf, from May 15, 1917 until April 4, 1922, during the anti-German feeling of World War I. Germantown became a city in 1959, and its population climbed from about 500 to just over 40,000 over the following decades while leaders used development rules and design controls to manage growth.

Old Germantown centers on the railroad depot on Germantown Road, rebuilt in 1948 to replace the 1868 original and now home to a train museum. Fort Germantown, off Poplar Pike, is on the National Register, and the John Gray House in Municipal Park predates 1851.

Is Germantown still growing?

Germantown has leveled off. The Census Bureau counted 38,844 people in 2010 and 41,333 in 2020, and its July 2025 estimate is 40,001, which is 3.2 percent below the 2020 base. Land area is 19.99 square miles, and density was 2,068 people per square mile in 2020.

With 2,068 residents per square mile and a shrinking head count, Germantown is a city where houses change hands one at a time rather than in big new subdivisions.

What do Census numbers show for Germantown homes?

Germantown is a city of homeowners. QuickFacts lists an owner-occupied rate of 86.7 percent, well above Franklin at 63.8 percent and Gallatin at 57.1 percent, with 15,568 households and 2.60 people per household. The median home value is $470,800 for 2020 to 2024. Median owner costs are $2,546 a month with a mortgage and $923 without one, and median gross rent is $1,816.

Median household income is $149,920, and 71.9 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher. Residents 65 and older make up 24.2 percent of the population, and 92.3 percent lived in the same house one year earlier.

Which school systems serve Germantown houses?

Germantown is served by two public systems, which matters when a buyer asks which school a given address feeds. The city runs its own Germantown Municipal School District, and three campuses inside the city limits remain with Shelby County Schools.

  • Germantown Municipal School District: Dogwood, Farmington and Forest Hill elementary schools, Riverdale K-8, Houston Middle School and Houston High School
  • Shelby County Schools: Germantown Elementary, Germantown Middle and Germantown High, an International Baccalaureate school
  • Private options: Evangelical Christian School, St. George's Independent School, The Bodine School, Our Lady of Perpetual Help and others

Because the two systems overlap, a seller should confirm the zoned school with the district before putting a line about it in a listing.

What does Germantown property tax cost and when is it due?

The city rate is $1.7825 per $100 of assessed value. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value, commercial at 40 percent and personal property at 30 percent. The Shelby County Assessor's Office does the valuations and gives the city a certified tax roll each October. Property tax produces about half of the revenue for city services.

The city is barred from giving relief on penalties. An owner who has not received a statement by early December can email Tax@Germantown-TN.gov or call 901-757-7218, and escrowed owners should pass the statement to their lender.

Shelby County sets its own appeal path. A request for an informal review at the assessor's office closes on the last day of May. The county Board of Equalization takes appeals from May 1 through June 30 with no filing fee, online or by mail, and a later step goes to the State Board of Equalization and then Shelby County Chancery Court. The 2026 filing window closed on June 30, 2026, and the board's page says it opens again each May 1.

What do code compliance and permits mean for a Germantown sale?

The Economic and Community Development Department, at 1920 S. Germantown Road, runs planning, public art and code compliance. Its Code Compliance officers enforce the Code of Ordinances, and staff there also support the Planning, Design Review, Public Art and Economic Development commissions and the Board of Zoning Appeals. Three city resources matter most to a seller:

  • A residential ordinance guide covering noise, parking, pet ownership and signage
  • Property maintenance standards for landscaping, trash disposal, exterior upkeep and nuisance prevention
  • Project guidelines and permit information for additions, fences and similar improvements

Before listing, call Code Compliance at 901-757-7281 and ask whether any open case is attached to the address. A sale can go smoothly or stall on that single question, and a seller who knows the answer can price the house with it in mind.

How is a Germantown deed recorded in Shelby County?

Germantown deeds are recorded by the Shelby County Register of Deeds, 1075 Mullins Station Road, Suite W165, Memphis, phone 901-222-8100. The office says a deed is usually recorded and mailed back in about one business day, with a digital copy online. Individuals cannot open an e-filing account on their own, and the office recommends a real estate professional who already has one. A quit claim deed typically costs about $12 to file.

If an owner has died without a probated will, the register notes that Tennessee requires one Affidavit of Heirship filed with its office, and that title companies often prefer three. Probate questions go to the Shelby County Probate Court Clerk at 901-222-3750.

The state's realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of purchase price, paid by the grantee at recording, and the register collects it for the Department of Revenue.

The Census Bureau estimated 40,001 residents in July 2025, down from 41,333 in the 2020 census.

The city of Germantown rate is $1.7825 per $100 of assessed value. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of appraised value.

When are Germantown property taxes due?

Taxes are due December 1, and payments must be postmarked by the last day of February to avoid state-mandated penalties. The city cannot waive those penalties.

What share of Germantown homes are owner-occupied?

About 86.7 percent, according to Census QuickFacts for 2020 to 2024. The median owner-occupied home value is $470,800.

Who records a deed for a Germantown house?

The Shelby County Register of Deeds in Memphis records it. Call 901-222-8100, and expect the document back in about one business day.

What is the fastest way to sell a Cookeville, TN house?

Handing the house to a direct cash buyer moves fastest in Cookeville, since the buyer's loan, the appraisal and weekend showings drop out. An agent listing may fetch more for a house in good repair, at the cost of prep time.

Cookeville is Putnam County's seat and biggest city, perched on the Highland Rim in the Upper Cumberland. The Census Bureau counted 34,842 residents in 2020 and estimates 38,212 for July 1, 2025. Sellers here range from landlords with student tenants to families settling a parent's house.

  • Cash sale: fits a house with deferred repairs or a lease still running.

  • Owner sale: fits someone who wants to run the negotiation and contract personally.

Whichever you pick, get a mortgage payoff letter and tax balances from both the city and the county before agreeing to a date.

What makes the Cookeville housing market different from other Tennessee cities?

The Census numbers show a college town. Just 41.1% of housing units are owner-occupied, far below the 48.0% Census figure for Cleveland, and households average 2.21 people. Rent runs a median $917 a month, and an owned home at the midpoint is valued at $305,400.

How do Cookeville's elevation, lakes and rainfall affect a house?

At about 1,100 feet, Cookeville sits a few hundred feet above Nashville and Knoxville, so heat and humidity run slightly lower. It lies near the crossroads of Interstate 40, State Route 136 and U.S. 70N, roughly 79 miles east of Nashville and 101 miles west of Knoxville.

The Corps of Engineers runs three nearby lakes, Center Hill, Cordell Hull and Dale Hollow. Closer in are City Lake and Burgess Falls Lake along the Falling Water River, and Cane Creek Lake in the west of town. Cookeville averages 60.02 inches of precipitation a year and 6.1 inches of snow.

  • U.S. 70N crosses downtown as Spring Street and, farther west, West Broad Street.
  • North Washington Avenue and South Jefferson Avenue carry traffic north and south.
  • Willow Avenue runs beside Tennessee Tech University.
  • Interstate Drive follows I-40 on the south side with hotels and chain restaurants.

In a wet climate, inspectors check roofs, gutters, crawl spaces and drainage first, so have a plain account of any past water trouble ready.

Who is buying houses in Cookeville?

Tennessee Tech University has been in Cookeville since 1915 and anchors the housing demand near Willow Avenue. Wikipedia also lists a Volunteer State Community College campus and Tennessee Bible College in town. Putnam County Schools, with Cookeville High School among the state's larger high schools, is a major employer as well.

Manufacturing leads the local economy with over 100 plants, with retail and health care next. The Cookeville Regional Medical Center, Averitt Express and Cummins appear among the city's largest employers. Cookeville is also the hub of a seven-county labor market, so some buyers commute in from surrounding towns.

None of this promises a fast listing sale, but it explains the steady interest from landlords and investors in houses near the campus and the hospital.

Where did Cookeville start, and does the history matter to a seller?

Cookeville takes its name from Richard Fielding Cooke, who settled in the area in 1810 and later served in the state senate. Putnam County was formed in 1842 and re-established in 1854, when state law required a county seat. Land bought by Charles Crook became that seat because natural springs could support a town.

The terrain explains why. The rugged Cookeville area suited large farms less well than much of Middle Tennessee, and the local economy leaned on logging, timber and smaller farms before manufacturing and the university took over. If your own lot has a history of wet ground or spring flow, tell the buyer early and offer any survey you hold.

What are the Cookeville and Putnam County tax deadlines?

Two bills arrive. The Putnam County Trustee collects county tax only, and the City of Cookeville collects its own tax at City Hall, 45 E Broad Street. The trustee reports a 2025 county rate of $2.66 per $100 of assessed value, which the County Commission sets, usually in July.

The county's payment window opens the first Monday of October and closes with the last day of February. March 1 starts interest at 1.5% a month, and anything still owed goes to Chancery Court on March 31. The Clerk and Master then collects delinquent county taxes and runs tax sales. The city follows a similar calendar: its notice for 2023 taxes set a 4:30 p.m. deadline on March 31, 2025, with no postmarks accepted, after which the Clerk and Master took over collection.

The trustee's page says taxes are typically prorated at closing and that the office does not do the proration, so rely on your closing company. The county trustee's number is 931-526-8845, and the Cookeville property tax office is at 931-520-5250.

Can older or disabled Cookeville owners get property tax relief?

Yes. The state repays part of the tax for qualifying homeowners, and Putnam County describes three tracks on its Trustee page.

  • Elderly or disabled homeowners: age 65 by December 31, or totally and permanently disabled, with combined income under $38,470.
  • Tax freeze: age 65 or older with household income at or below $42,200.
  • Disabled veterans and surviving spouses who meet the listed disability categories.

Relief applies only to a primary residence and is a state payment, not an exemption. Recipients must pay in the office or by mail, since banks cannot take relief payments. If you are selling a home you have been getting relief on, ask the trustee how the sale affects your application.

What happens to the deed when a Cookeville house sells?

The Putnam County Register of Deeds records the new deed. State recordation tax combines a realty transfer tax with a mortgage tax, and the revenue department explains on its recordation tax page that the register collects both and sends the money to the state.

Ask the Putnam County Register of Deeds for the present recording fee and any document requirements. When a house has been inherited or has multiple owners, have the closing company confirm who must sign. The Clerk and Master's office in Chancery Court handles matters such as partition and quiet title, which can arise when ownership is unclear.

More questions about Cookeville, TN

Can I sell my Cookeville house with tenants still living in it?

Yes. With renters in most Cookeville homes, tenant-occupied sales are common. Give the buyer the lease and deposit details, and ask your closing company how the deposit moves at closing.

When are Putnam County property taxes due?

They are payable from the first Monday in October through the last day of February without interest. Interest of 1.5% per month starts March 1.

Does the county trustee also collect Cookeville city tax?

No. The Putnam County Trustee collects county tax only. City tax is paid at Cookeville City Hall, 45 E Broad Street.

What happens to unpaid Cookeville property tax?

Unpaid county tax goes to Chancery Court on March 31 and the Clerk and Master collects it with added fees and interest. The city sends its own unpaid taxes there too after its deadline.

Who prorates property tax at a Cookeville closing?

Your closing company does. The Putnam County Trustee states it does not prorate taxes between buyers and sellers, so ask your closing agent how the year is split.

What makes selling a house in Bristol, TN different?

Bristol is a Sullivan County city that shares a state line, a main street and a regional economy with Bristol, Virginia, with State Street as the dividing line. The two cities keep separate governments, police departments and libraries, so a Tennessee seller deals with Tennessee offices only.

QuickFacts estimates 28,107 residents for July 1, 2025, a 3.7 percent gain on the April 2020 estimates base. Bristol is a principal city in the Kingsport to Bristol metro area and the wider Tri-Cities region. Bristol Motor Speedway, a NASCAR track, and the Bristol Rhythm and Roots Reunion each September bring visitors, though neither sets what an ordinary house is worth.

What does the federal data say about Bristol housing?

It describes an older, lower-cost market with a sizable renter share. Adults past 65 make up 19.5 percent of the population, household income in the middle of the range is $58,162, and typical rent is $842 a month.

How are Bristol property taxes set after the 2025 reappraisal?

A Bristol house is taxed by two governments: Sullivan County and the City of Bristol, Tennessee. For tax year 2025 the county commission kept its rate at $1.6129 per hundred dollars of assessed value, which was the state-certified figure replacing a 2024 rate of $2.4962, while the city council adopted $1.87, according to a January 2026 county newsletter. The reappraisal reset values, so the state certified a revenue-neutral city rate of $1.5397. The council chose $1.87, which the county calculates as 21.45 percent above that certified level. The 2024 city rate had been $2.25 on the older values.

The county assessor runs a countywide reappraisal every two years, and the next is scheduled for 2027. For a house valued at $194,500, residential assessment at 25 percent gives $48,625 of assessed value, which at those combined rates comes to roughly $1,694 a year. Use your own notice for the exact amount.

Where do I pay Sullivan County taxes and what relief exists?

The 2025 bills could be paid until February 27, 2026, and the Trustee's main office is at 3411 Highway 126, Suite 104, Blountville, phone 423-323-6464. A Bristol office operates on Thursdays and Fridays from October 1 through March 13 at the Ralph Harr Justice Center, 801 Anderson Street, Room 139, phone 423-354-7037.

The county also runs a payment plan that splits an expected bill into ten equal monthly payments beginning in March. The same newsletter describes the state's tax relief program for older, disabled and veteran homeowners. For 2025 taxes the income cap was $37,530 based on 2024 income, with an additional $85 rebate from the county for elderly and disabled participants.

  • Homeowners older than 65 can qualify if combined income, including a spouse or co-owner, is within the cap.
  • Disabled homeowners recognized by the Social Security Administration use the same income cap.

Ask the Trustee which year's limits apply before you file.

What is the route for challenging a Sullivan County value?

Call the assessor, Donna Whitaker, at 3411 Highway 126, Suite 103, Blountville, phone 423-323-6455, and go to the county equalization board if her answer leaves you unconvinced. The assessor's page notes that the office does not set the tax rate, send the bill or collect payment, so a rate complaint goes elsewhere.

The state's appeal guide says a dispute generally has to reach the local board first. If you disagree with that ruling, the state filing is due by August 1 of the tax year or 45 days after the local notice, whichever is later. Hearings before an administrative judge turn on evidence, and the guide names comparable sales as the best proof for a house.

While a challenge is open, the state expects the undisputed portion of the tax to be paid before the delinquency date, and unpaid amounts can bring penalties or a dismissal.

What local housing news affects Bristol sellers?

Council notices show where the city is steering development. In March 2026 the council held a public hearing on an ordinance for a temporary moratorium on establishing permanent campgrounds, and it took up a resolution supporting a workforce housing development to be built by DP Builders. Those items appear on the city's legal notices page, which also posts hearings on budgets and tax rates.

Bristol Tennessee City Schools serves nearly all of the city, with Tennessee High School as its public high school, and a small section falls under Sullivan County Schools. King University is a Bristol institution. The city's weather runs cooler than most of Tennessee: around 41 inches of yearly precipitation and 13.3 inches of normal winter snowfall, with 17 days a year reaching 90 degrees or higher. Roofs, gutters and furnaces take the wear that kind of weather brings, and a buyer with a mortgage may ask for repairs before closing.

For zoning questions on a particular lot, call the Department of Development Services before you plan a rental or an addition, since use rules differ by district. Council meetings are held at the Slater Community Center, 325 McDowell Street, and the legal notices page lists agendas ahead of time.

How is a Bristol sale recorded and taxed?

Bristol deeds are filed in Blountville with the Sullivan County Register of Deeds, 3411 Highway 126, Suite 101, phone 423-323-6420, where the counter is staffed from 8 in the morning until 4:30 on weekdays. The Department of Revenue sets the state transfer tax at 37 cents per $100 of price, about $720 on a $194,500 sale.

Have the title company prorate the year's property tax on the closing statement.

  • Gather a payoff letter from each lienholder before closing.
  • Confirm who signs for any estate or co-owner situation.
  • Check the Trustee's record for unpaid prior-year taxes, which the title company will expect to see settled at closing.

More questions about Bristol, TN

How much is the Bristol, TN property tax rate?

For tax year 2025 the city levies $1.87 per hundred dollars of assessed value and the county levies $1.6129, which totals $3.4829. Both figures come from the county's January 2026 newsletter. Rates are set annually, so confirm the current numbers with the Trustee.

When are Sullivan County property taxes due?

Bills for 2025 could be paid through February 27, 2026 at the bank locations, and the Trustee's own deadline was the end of that month. The Blountville office answers at 423-323-6464. Ask for the interest schedule on late payments.

Can I sell a Bristol house with unpaid taxes?

Yes. Back taxes are normally paid from your proceeds at the closing table. Ask the Sullivan County Trustee for the current balance before choosing a date.

Where is the Bristol Tennessee Register of Deeds?

It sits at 3411 Highway 126, Suite 101, in Blountville, and the phone number is 423-323-6420. Weekday hours run from 8 am to 4:30 pm, except on designated holidays.

Is Bristol, Tennessee the same as Bristol, Virginia?

No. They are two cities with separate governments that share a border at State Street. A house on the Tennessee side uses Sullivan County offices, Tennessee law and Tennessee taxes.

Where is Farragut, Tennessee, and who lives there?

Farragut is a suburban town in Knox County with a small extension into Loudon County, part of the Knoxville metro area. The Town's own facts page gives its size as 16.2 square miles. Interstate 40/75 forms most of the northern edge, Turkey Creek Road and the Norfolk Southern rail line mark the south, the Loudon County line is the west boundary, and Lovell Road plus the Concord Hills subdivisions close off the east.

The 2020 census counted 23,506 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 25,121, a gain of 6.9 percent. Median age in 2020 was 46.7, and 23.7 percent of people were 65 or older. Married couples headed 70.8 percent of the 8,521 households. Of 8,992 housing units, 5.2 percent sat vacant, with a 1.5 percent vacancy rate among owner homes and 14.3 percent among rentals.

Those figures come from the census and the Town's facts page, and they are a useful backdrop for anyone weighing a sale of a Farragut house.

How did Farragut become a town?

The area began as Campbell's Station, a fort and stagecoach stop built by Captain David Campbell in 1787. The brick Campbell's Station Inn went up in 1810 and still stands on Kingston Pike within sight of Town Hall. The Battle of Campbell's Station was fought here on November 16, 1863. The town takes its name from Union Admiral David Farragut, who was born just east of here in 1801.

Incorporation came late. In December 1979 the Knoxville City Council voted to annex stretches of I-40 right-of-way in the Farragut area, and residents petitioned for an incorporation election. Farragut voted to incorporate on January 16, 1980, which blocked further annexation by Knoxville. Bob Leonard was elected the first mayor on April 1, 1980.

What does the land and climate mean for a Farragut house?

Farragut sits in hilly ground between Blackoak Ridge to the north and Fort Loudoun Lake on the Tennessee River to the south, at about 936 feet above sea level. Hills mean sloped lots, and sloped lots mean buyers and inspectors pay attention to drainage, retaining walls and foundations.

The Town reports these climate averages:

  • Annual precipitation of 47.86 inches and about 6 inches of snow
  • January highs near 46 degrees and July highs near 88
  • A freeze-free period averaging 214 days
  • Prevailing winds from the southwest

Nearly 48 inches of rain a year puts roofs, gutters and crawl spaces on every inspection list. A seller who has patched a leak or regraded a yard should keep the receipts for the buyer.

What does property tax look like for a Farragut homeowner?

Farragut levies no municipal property tax. Residents pay Knox County's rate of $1.55 per $100 of assessed value, and the Town reports that residential property is assessed at 25 percent of market value and commercial at 40 percent. Knox County sales tax is 9.25 percent, or 5.25 percent on groceries.

For a house valued at $600,000, the assessed value would be $150,000, and $1.55 per $100 yields $2,325 a year. That sum is an illustration built from the published rate, so check the actual bill on the trustee's site.

The Knox County Property Assessor reappraises on a two-year schedule and mails a notice whenever an assessed value changes. An owner who disagrees can appeal to the County Board of Equalization when it meets in June. The assessor also says that after a deed is recorded, its system can take up to a week to show the new owner.

Which permits and code rules affect a Farragut sale?

Farragut's Building and Fire Codes Division enforces the adopted building, plumbing, gas, mechanical, housing, swimming pool and fire codes. A permit is needed for most remodeling. Water heater change-outs, HVAC replacements and any gas appliance installation require permits and inspections through the Town, and mechanical applications must include a Manual J report. Electrical inspections run through the Lenoir City Utilities Board.

Work that skips a permit is the usual snag at closing, so it helps to confirm what was permitted before listing. Items on the Town's no-permit list include one-story detached sheds up to 200 square feet and fences up to 7 feet, though zoning approval may still apply.

Code enforcement follows a set path:

  • A complaint is reviewed and an officer does a drive-by inspection.
  • A courtesy notice goes to the owner, usually with a 10-day deadline, though it can range from immediate to 30 days.
  • If the problem persists, the owner can be cited to Municipal Court, where fines reach $50 per day per violation.
  • The Town may fix the problem itself and place a lien on the property for the cost.

A seller with an open notice should call Town Hall at 865-966-7057 before accepting any offer, because a lien would have to be dealt with at closing.

Which schools and roads shape demand in Farragut?

Most Farragut addresses are zoned to Knox County Schools: Farragut Primary (K-2), Farragut Intermediate (3-5), Farragut Middle (6-8) and Farragut High (9-12), with Northshore Elementary also serving the area. Part of the town north of I-75 is zoned for Hardin Valley Middle and Hardin Valley Academy. Knoxville Christian School and Concord Christian School are private options.

Kingston Pike, the merged US 70 and US 11, runs through the middle of town, and I-40/75 runs along its northern edge. The town lists commuting links to Oak Ridge, Knoxville, Maryville, Alcoa and McGhee Tyson Airport, and a commuter lot at Campbell Station Road and Campbell Lakes Drive serves ride sharers. Gas comes from the Knoxville Utilities Board, electricity from the Lenoir City Utility Board, and fire protection is subscription-based through Rural Metro.

A buyer who learns about the Rural Metro subscription early will not be surprised by it at closing.

How does a Farragut house sale move from offer to recorded deed?

An owner can list with an agent, sell directly to a buyer, or take a cash offer from a company that buys houses as-is. A cash sale suits a house that needs work, carries a code notice, or has a deadline attached. Whatever route is chosen, the deed is recorded in Knox County, not at Town Hall.

The Knox County Register of Deeds says a deed should be recorded as soon as possible, though no statutory time limit exists, and that signatures must be notarized or witnessed by two people. Documents are usually recorded the same day received. Tennessee's realty transfer tax is $0.37 per $100 of the purchase price, and the Department of Revenue says the grantee pays it when the deed is recorded.

The assessor will send a sales questionnaire after ownership changes, including a private sale or a transfer into a trust. Sellers should also tell the trustee where to mail later bills. Ask the Knox County Trustee how any current-year balance is handled at closing.

More questions about Farragut, TN

Does Farragut have its own property tax?

No. The Town of Farragut levies no municipal property tax, and residents pay the Knox County rate of $1.55 per $100 of assessed value. Residential property is assessed at 25 percent of market value.

Where is a Farragut deed recorded?

At the Knox County Register of Deeds in Suite 225 of the City County Building, 400 Main Street, Knoxville. Call 865-215-2330. Each county records only the real estate inside its own borders.

Do I need a permit to replace a water heater in Farragut?

Yes. The Town of Farragut requires a permit and inspection for water heater change-outs, HVAC replacements and gas appliance installations. Contact the Codes office at 865-966-7057 or 865-675-2384 if you are unsure.

What happens if Farragut sends me a code courtesy notice before I sell?

Respond before the deadline, usually 10 days. If the issue is still open at the follow-up inspection, the owner can be cited to Municipal Court, with fines up to $50 per day per violation, and the Town can place a lien after fixing the problem.

Who is the transfer tax paid by on a Farragut sale?

The buyer, as grantee. Tennessee charges $0.37 per $100 of purchase price when the deed is recorded, and the Register of Deeds collects it for the Department of Revenue.
